But the most liberal sheep farmer cannot do without the shepherd's love. and this is not a Comm. gift. An Australian sheep farmer used to say that he had ten shepherds, all convicts. One w3B a clergyman. Ile yeas idle, sat d.iwn, and let the sheep wamler. Another was all English shepherd. He could 1 nut adapt himself hi the vagrant ways of colonial sheep' Another ifaS a munlerer. He drove the sheep too hard. The best al the whole ten was a London piektooket. In the I exercise of his profession he had been olis,vant, and dexterous, taking constant note of persons, peculiarities, , and dress. He had had to estimate the value of his victims, and to obtain his object with the kast disturhance to their sensibilities. He watched the sheep carefully, knew what each had in its pocket, and did his best to secure the prize for his employer. Such is the power of personal attention and discrimination. This can be taught in a better school than that in which the poor pickpocket acquired his train- ing. It is one id the special accomplishments of good so- ciety, and certain it is that if any one is rude, hard, and in- considerate to the poor brutne placed in his power he is likely to lits to his human surroundings also. Proctor, the astronomer, who is now travelling in America, writee to the Newcastle Chroroielt travelling in parts of America woold be much lees tote then ill, were it not for certain Indian superstitions. Although there have been instances in which rgilway trains have been thrown off the track and plundered by Indians, yet in general , they regard the mysterious fire.horees an under the protec- tion of the Great Spirit, and refrain religiously from molest- ,Mg them. The telegraphic wires and poles are also left untouched. 'There is, I hell-ye, only one care on record in which an Indian ever ventured to break telegraph poles or wirm. A young Sioux Indian determined to show hie cour- age and also his contempt for the" medicine" of the white ma, cut dawn with bit hatchet one of the telegraph poles. By lucky chance (considering what really serious issues depended on the experiment) a severe thunderstorm was in progress of some distance. and a charge of electricity, taken up by the wires, was passed to the pole which the Indian was cutting, and he wee instantaneously killed. After that no Indians have moleeted wires, and doubtless railway rreim also are regarded now try thetn at under the hnmediate pro- tection of the Great Spirit. This euperstition singularly illontrates the feet that some errors are best left uncorrecteri. Truth is not at all Hines profitable. Any one who, in his anxiety to eorrect error, should explain to the untutored mind of the "poor Indian " the rml nature of telegraphic communication, steam engines, Ac, and show clearly how the young Sioux came by hie death, would probably came the death of hundreda of poor white folk, and the destruction of • large ammint of property, during the next few years. And in like mintier, I imagine that considerable mischief might be done if the precise truth were taught reepect inn some other snperelitione nearer home, and by many regarded ae altogether inner respectable than the life-racing eupereti.. Hone of the Indians. Fortunately, there is very little chance, either in one We the other, that ignorance and euperstition will been easily removed, The Indian, at any rate, will either be tamed or civilised off the face of the earth before he will be persuaded that neither telegraphic communication one railmati travelling are supernaturally toought about and Impernaturally protected. He would reply much as Black Beaver replied to General M.o.cy at Si. LAW!, "Injurt not yety arnaht, sometimes he big fool ; but l'epect you try to fool me now. Mop'c Poe lie."

She took knitting needles and wool with her, intending to add usefulness too quiet gossip. Nothing more RaA heurl od her at home that diy. and a messenger being despatched ou the following dry to the house of Lachan' ce he learned the .dartling news that no one there had heard of her at all. A search at once instituted, and it was without avail for A long time. At length the erarchere found footprints leading to a well, and near by traces of a desperate struggle. Further on they none to the well, and to their horror discovered the bode, head down- wards, in it. Upon being brought to the sniface it was die- onvered that the had been outraged and bruised in a horrible manner. Her face was gashed, with knife wounds, and from !several slashes in her throat and head blood was oozing. Her hands were mat with a knife, And these wounds, with her torn clothes, showed how deadly must have been her struggles for honour and life. The body was taken power- aion of by the authorities, yet up to the latent hour no news has been heard as to the assassin. Suspicion points too pedlar, who had been seen in the neighbourhood with a torn coat and blood marks upon his fare, but nn arrests have been made, and mystery reigns supreme aloof the dreadful deed. !or justice moves with sluggish feet in these Canadian vit. lages. Justice Denman heard at the Liverpool assiree, on Saturday, an action sent down for trial front the Court of Chancery to decide whether the plaintiff, John Piere, , was the son .f John Pierce, sen., who died in Liverpool in ISfid. The formation of a coalition between the Con.rvatives and the two impasseet gr,ups of the Left, headed respectively by Signor Crispi and BATOil.Nicotera, ie regarded as almost certain; and such h combination would probably be able to accomplieh the irn- : mediate downfall of the Cairoli Adminintration. Theme Cabinet crises, which are becoming chronic in Italy, arise I Iron the want of organic unity nn the part of the Left. The parte is anti, up into coteries, each of nhtiet, ho ire own chief it hoe no recognised leader, end the Prime Minister for the tisne being is liable to be defeated at any moment by the withdrawal of a dieaffected section under the disinte- grating inE.nce of merely personal Jealousies. The Italian Press ban been goodly struck by the absence of these pont,- ful personal rivalries in the English Liberal party and the example of Lord Hartington and Lord Granville in cheer- fully making way for Mr. Gladstone, because they regarded him an the natural Liberal leader, has formed a fruitfol text for sermons to Italian politicians There seems to be con- siderable ground for the complaint that Italy still only pos- se.. the skeleton of Parliamentary government. RUSSIA. The London correspondent of the Leeds Mercury write,: —A friend who has returned from the hulalien Principali- ties tells me that a war between Russia and Austria is con- sidered only a question of time. This is the danger to which Lord Beaconsfield teferrsl in his extraordinary manifesto. ft was well known that Austria hos secured a position in the Balkans which endang,rs the supremacy of Russia there. The latter Power is preparing for contingencits by getting the Bulgarian army in order, the assistance of Bulg.tria being, of course, secured by Russia. Roumania, on the other band, sides with Austria, and M. Bridal., the Roumanian Premier, recently gave a personal assurance to that effect at Vienna. Great activity prevails in the Austrian army. It remains to be seen what effect the change of Government in this country may hare on the state of affairs. The Russians will doubtless count upon the countenance, if not the direct aid, of Mr. Gladstone, whilst the Austrians are &Ware that he will oppose them Should Attatria secure the active support of Germany, then the defeat of Russia is cerhtin.

1 right for hard cosh, or for . muw of the primest Wilderspool brew, bought with Radical money, may be accepted without question. Several humorous re- ports of the way in which the " private sporting gentlemen from Liverpool wore befouled by ineceoctee Moriva related to them, for the purpose of "drawing them on," reached to whilst the "gentlemen' were in quest of " cases ; ' but we have not the : space to repeat them here even if any purpose could be served by doing it. The "private gentle- rare," of !Your., understood their mission so far as it ' cone trned themeelv., and, in common parlance, "to keep the pot boiling" they reported " " which made the lights of Toryism rub their hands with glee land talk glibly of being in posseesion of facts that : would un.at Mr. MeMinuiem The "private gentle- ' men " laughed in their sleeves as they witnessed the " wire-pullers " iarried to the acme of felicity by the mental gyration. the reports of " cases " produced, and in which the deluded ones conjured up fancies of Ithe assembling a "big-wigs," the torturing of I witness., the "shocking disci...," and the die- , comfitme of the Radicals in the unseating of. their : admired champion. The defeated baronet, who has so often led Tory iom to victory, and who pretended not to be disconcerted by his defeat, but simply in sorrow over the lamentations of his followers, was Aectrified into unusuld activity. llis ingoinge and outgoings were accomplished with a al:dinginess of step second only to the agility of a juvenile acrobat, whilst his countenance resumed the radiant smiles that were dissipated on the lad ult, by the mournful tones that worked their way by centortioaa up the stale. ease of the Lion Hotel "Why, we're 529 on the wrong ! side ! " Somebody's cash box was opened, and the private gentlemen," in their employer.' felicitous moments, were made happy by well!filled purees. But the hour of refliction came even to the "private gentlemen," and the question how to "keep the pot boiling" .eumed with them a aeriouve. that touched them to the quick. There were too many " bogus. " in their "cases" to permit of the j oyottextees of their employere and of their own harvest Imting, and & de- termined effort was made to find a genuine "case." " sinners " th, y had whispered soft pleadings to in vain, and they resolved to get the better of" pub. beans." They laid siege to a Bonifaos whom they endeavoured to persuade had fed and fuddled nearly the whole of the Liberal following on the day of elec- tion ; and imagining that they had, by their—s7l t impeachments, hoodwinked the Knight of the Spigot into the belief that be had been in dreamland when be denied all knowledge of gnotnitons fried-ham and beer for all comers to his house on the day of the contest, they strove to wheedle hint into a confeeition of a horrible tale of corruption. Money was no object with each a confession at stake. A bandfultf gold and a batch of bank notes were produced by one of the " private " sporting gentlemen as evidence that he w. prepared 1 for businese, but even the promise of £lOO to Boniface to " split " failod tosecure • genuine "case." With pocket-booke fall of entries utterly worthiese except to fan the bliss of their employers, and in fear of a collnpae of a profitable mission they were anMouit to 1 prolong, the " gentlemen " were occasionally , found dodging round street corners, or on sentry at a public-honoe window, looking for some of the :seventeen detectives they supposed had been engaged In watching their movements, but of whom no one I knew anything but the very" private gentlemen" in . quest of "cases" to keep Tory delight buoyant. The air was charged with rumour upon rumour of the terrible havoc the wire-pullers of Cometvatism believed thematicrs capable of making with the Liberal victory, but the departure of the 'priests gentlemen" to their old sporting haunts opened the door for the admisiti,ta of thewet blanket that smothered the boastings and crowing of the deluded. To admit that they had been cajoled, befouled, bamboozled by ft welchers " is more than o.ald be expected from ;Tory wire -pullere on finding their cashbox lighter and 1 reams of paper covered with trumped-up eases of 1 bribery, evolved from the inner consciousnese of the "gentlemen "• of the turf. The body and tail of outraged Conservatism had, for all that, ' to be appeased, and that without ehowing how the head had permitted itself to get into "chancery." 1 A mild course of treatment was resolved upon. The head first resolved that it had been humbugged —thoroughly humbugged. Then it wen resolved that, though there was no cam, it would be a piece of tomfoolery lousy so. Next it was resolved that, for the credit of the head, the body and tail should be: 1 led to still believe in the existence of genuine cases of Radical bribery, but that for the sake of peace and to avoid the appearance of spleen vs the outcome of • licking,- it um advisable to abandon the petition 1 so much time and money had been apart to get up in I order the Radicals might be worsted. Further it watt I resolved that the foregoing resolutions should be the guide to the writer of on " invited" article for a neutial contemporary, announcing the possibility of the petition toeing abandoned, and that the body and tail of the party ohould be summoned to meet the head on Monday evenicg last, where the reams of eupposed t• cases " had been put on the elle.oo to be hereafter labelled " mistakes."

IThe meeting was held. The tail wriggled with discontent, and the body waxed wrath at the proposal to abandon the petition ; but the head lulled suspicion by asking where the money to carry the petition through had to come from ? Sir Gilbert— the fountain of the Conservative sinews of war—who had been let into the secret of the worthlessness of the reams of " cases " and the smartness of the "private gentlemen," declared his intention to button up his pocket; nod as from head to tad not a soul present would risk more than a sovereign, there waa nothing for it but to fall in with the inevitable—the abandon- ment of the petition. The proceedings at this caucus meeting were other• wine interesting. It was soberly contended that the "ticking' on the 2ud ultimo demonstrated that the Conservative party needed reorganising. How it should be done woo a bone of contention, and the "happy family" woe found to contain in it four rivals for the mayoralty. A quiet spectator nays the meeting was ".11 at five's and tines,' and that there will be a heap of political dry bones as noon as the baronet of Walton Hall hoe closed his purse. The curtain had better be drawn here. We can stand anything better than dry bones.

&stone Conservati•e journals have from time to time industriously cultivated the idea that Conservative states- men only find favour at the Court, and that Her Majeaty for sonic reason or other hod contracted an invincible dislike to Mr. Gladstone and other shitennell connected with the Liberal party. The wish, however, has been father to the thought, and the man whom it Ilan been sought to humiliate is at this moment the most trueted and honoured among his fellows. The late Lord Derby once f;ublicly declared that the Queen would never permit Mr. Bright, the *People's Tribune,' le become a minleter of the Crown, and when the bon. gentleman did become a minister Her Majesty, and other member. of the Royal Family, took particular care to show to the Quaker statesman marked attention, as if to resent the unwarrantable asaertion of the noble Earl. We have authority to' —7iog that the Conservative press have had no more authority for proclaiming the dislike of the members of the Royal Family to Mr. Gladstone than the late Earl of Derby heel for asserting that Mr. Bright would find no favour at Court. It is undoubtedly true that on the occasion of the marriage of the Duke of Connaught, Mr.! Gladstone was the only prominent statesman who was not invited to the wedding, hut, if this We, intended an a slight —a pitiful proceeding at best—we fancy the responsibility lies more at the door of the Court minions than at the foot of the throne. The Queen has too much good sense to slight the man whom the nation chooses to honour : indeed we know that the Freruier has denied receiving, at any time, at the hands of Her Majesty anything but the most courteous treatment • sovereign could extend to a subject. In the crowds which have during the present week gathered about 1 the approaches to Mr. Gladstone's I.ndon residence, sad, which have followed him and cheered him as be has pro- ceeded through the atreets of the metropolis, there is an evidence of the popularity of Mr. Gladstone that permeates the whole country, and which the Sovereign would not not yen- memo to eine to gratify a personal whim.

I Now that all the constituencies have given the verdicts it is interesting to note how the electors of the United Kingdom have spoken through the batted boo an the policy of the Lite Government. That policy has met with over- whelming condemnation. At the dissolution at Easter the Beaconsfield Cabinet had at its back in the Boone of ICommons a majority of 54. That majority has been dispelled, and the new Liberal Government hoe come into power with a majority of proferaing Liberals numbering 113. It to this number the 54 Home Rulers who bare been elected are added the change of position of parties in the Home of Commons Is represented by it Liberal majority

Tor figures 529 reprennt the number of stalks of wormwood in the quiver, of the wire pullers of Con- servatism in Warrington. A whopping inthe ballot boo by a force exceeding in own by 529 voters, and that, too, of ter reigning supreme for over forty years, and feeling assured of perpetuating it. eupremacy, has proved too much for Warrington Conservatism, for it has writhed and plunged under the smarting blow, and been bilious to &painful degree, since the evening of the second ultimo. A memorable evening that will I be, long after the nauseousuen with which the politi- cal sufferers are afflicted has been classed with past ailments. The usually tweet silvery voice of Mr. Robert Davies, who had been chosen to pilot the Col, serrative ehip through the storm rei.iby the Liberals, sounded dolefully to it cork-screwed itaelf up the atair - case of the Lion Hotel and pierced the eara of Sir Gilbert Greenall with "Why, we're 529 on the wrong ode" That Sir Gilbert sought the aid of friendly chair, and that hie nephew "the saintly Edward," the Liverpool Tory champion, subeided into a corner with his arms crowed over his sanctified bosom, and with an exclamation of astonishment, are now matter. of history. Just as the head was affected by the powerful dose of Liberalism found in the ballot box, so the body and tail of local Conservatism were be- wildered. From tail to head Conservatism has been wriggling ever Pince, and the head has been bothered, by the pereistent way in which the tail has kept up the wriggle, how to prevent the body from falling to pieces. Liberalism might be beaten for half, cen- tury and be content to bear ita " lickinge " with resig- nation ; but Conservatirie—never ! If Conservatism is

firmahe'd there mind be treachery lurking somewhere. All the discreditable practicea by which Tory victsnies were won in the past must bare been copied by the enemy and multiplied a hundred•fold, and what is left of Conservatism must, of course, put on the puritanical cloak, and track the peacadilloes of those horrid Radicals until they themselves shout Peccavi !"

To be beaten by stick a erneking majority as .529 iron fair fight is more than Warrington Toryiam has been able to withstand or understand. The popularity of the Liberal champion, Kr. Mdifinnies, and the disgust of thoughtful people with the six years Of " glory and gunpowder" policy of the Beaconefield Government and all its depressing aseociationa, never seem to hare dawned upon themindsof the wire-pullers of the kcal Conservative party, end for a month past they have been engaged in a war-dance around a political mare's nest. It hoe been amusing to see how ! the fandango has been kept up, and the suddenneas with which the blasts of the war trumpet have been husked. The prepotency of Liberalism over Con• aerratiam, manifeated on the 2nd ultimo, proved ouch • " staggerer" that it was believed there was no chenee of redemption for Toryism unlit. the Liberal victor could be brought upon his marrow bones at a legal stool of repentance. and to pick hobo in the Radical coat a batch of sporting tbartierim, known as " welchere," arrayed in grey-tweed raiment, were imported from Liverpool under the style and title of " private detectives." Whether them gentry re- ceived apecifie instructions to aseettain if any agent of the Liberal candidate had imitated a Tory agent, who knew more about cobbling than electioneering, and who, on the morning of the election, made so great a show of the Tory gold entrusted to him that the money was taken from him, and he was given another commission, . we cannot pretend to over; but that they trotted slant from pillar to poet, endeavouring to discover " potwollorro," who hwi sold their kolitiowl birth-

of 177 voles. The counties, regarded as the strongholla of Toryism, hove done much to ePen,,,tJaen the ranks of the Liberals. The English and Welsh counties in 1874 sent only 33 Liberals to Parliament. Last manth they have returned 68, being a net gain of 35. The Scotch counties Inane also sent 9 more Liberals than they did in 1974. Leon' it out of the reckoning Orkney and Shetland the major itit, where Liberal victories have been weinwl average lido VOtCA. The 33 seats won from the Liberals by the Conservatives were secured by a gross majority Of only 3,178 votes, or an average majority uf 13$ for each seat. This gross majority has been more than wiped out by the Liheral majority in South-East Lancashire and in other single constituencies that could be named. Though the Conservatives Con. IWO office in 1874 with a strong majority a Larger number of Liberal yches were reghhered throughout the country than of Con- servative votes. In 1974 the total number of voters on the registers of the United hillgtlolll was 2,648,962 in 1680 this number had incremed to 3.038,726, being an augmenta- tion of 389,764. Inclusive of Home Rulers the number of Liberal voters polled in 1874 wan 830,552; the number of lone voters was 701,797. It will !semen that 1,116,6:3 not. In did not vote, and that of those who did vote there was a Liberal majority of 128,755. At the election just concluded the number of Liberal voters, including Home Rulere, was 1,246,669, against 871,346 Tory voters. The number of voters, therefore. who did net go to the pod wan 820,701. A much larger proportion, however, voted than in 1874, and there moan net Liberal gain of 298,266 votes, being one- third niore than the whole numb, of Tories who voted. Them statistics prove undeniably that the majority of the elm stool the country are in favour of a Liberal form of Governruent,and opposed to that policy of Imperialism tint Lord lieaconsfield has been endeavouring to persuade Li:,,- tell would find sanction at the pulling booths. He has by his slier dimornfiture been taught tlnit his high-down policy was a mistake, and he retires into private life with the mnviction that his official career ended inn failure. Whil,t the Tories succeeded in the recent elections in wresting from the Liberals only 2 seats gained by iliern in 1874,the Liberals in no less than 54 constituencies [list decided is favour of Toryism in 1874 have wholly or partially reversed the character of the representation. More contests ha, been fought 111.1 either in 1874 or 1508. The number of uncon- tested elections in the latter year was 211: in 1874, 181 ; this year, 76. The elections this year have resulted in funnishing Parliament with Conch "new blood:. Of the members elected 735 have not been in the House of Corn. mons previouely, and alimit two-tnirds of this number is made up of Liberaleend Home Rulers. Ti,, number of new members returned at the elections in 1874 was 212, and, in ; 18138, 228. Three "extraordinary " elections are yet to come off. One is to fill the vacancy occasioned at Nottingham by time lamented death of Mr. J. S. Wright. The other two will be at Radnor Burghs and Leeds, as die result of the double return of Lord Harlington and Mr. Gladstone. Since the above was written, Orkney and Shetland have pro- nounced in favour of the Liberal mindidate, Mr. Laing, who has been returned by a majority of 378. This will bring the total Liberal majority up to 178.

Mr. Gladstone has proved equal to the duty which hi. Sovereign has called upon him to perform. He has nucceeded in funning a Ministry which will give general satiafaction to the country. As in Ital, he has sumtnonol to Lis aid representatives of all nem ions of the Liberal party, and the Ministry of which he is chief embraces men with the most old fashioned of IVhig notions and some of the most ad- vanced thinkers of the Radical school. The readiness with which the repreeentatives of the different clown of Reformers have shown to put on artnour under the chieftaimliip of Mr. Gladstone is one of the highest testimonies of confidence in the veteran statesman that could be shown him. In bringing to the front the younger generation of statesmen, and recognising and incorporating in his Ministry all shmles of Liberal opinions, Mr. Gladstone bas shown a wisdom and breadth of liberality that redound to his honour, and which will unmistakably Im to the advantage of the Empire. Of the fourteen members of the newly-formed Cabinet, a few held office in the Cabinet of the last Liberal Adminis- tration ; but there in an infusion of much new blood that will Inane its effmt in the furtherance of needful legislation. Mr. Gladstone combinee in his own person the Mikes of Premier and Chancellor of the Exchetmer, and his acceptance of the management of the financial department is a guarantee to the country that fiscal matters will be more efficiently con- trolled than they have been diving the last six years. Lord Selborne resumes the office of Lord Chancellor, Willa he abandoned in 1874. Earl Spencer fills the office of Lord Free dent of the Council, held by Lord Aberdare in the last Liberal Cabinet, The Delte of Argyll, who was the Indian Secretary in Mr. Gladstonen last Government, takes the office of Lord Privy Seal, which was held by Lord Hal Ham and the Marquis of Harlington beeomes the 11131411 Secretary, an appointment that will give satisfaction to the whole Indian dependency. Mr. Lowe is no longer in office, and the pist he held an Home Secretary in 1574 will be filled be Sir William V. Harcourt, who possemes all the advantages of an efficient Horne Secretary• He is generally regarded an a man of ample knowledge and grort person it decision, and without these qualitim the Home Office often proves a source of weakness and embarrassment le the Government. Lad Granville returns to hG old post as Fureigo Secretary, a position which Inc proved himself no thoroughly qmlitied to till during the last Liberal Government. Earl Cardwell does not again take office, and to the pOnt he held as War Secretary Mr. Childers succeeds. The First Lord of the Admiralty is Lord North- brook : and Mr. limehen, who was the First Lord in the Liberal Administration that went out of office in 1074 will, in all probability, proceed to Constantinople as the successor to Sir Henry layard. Mr. Chaniberlain becomes President of the Board of Trade. and his appointment meets with the satisfaction of the Radical element of the Liberal party, as does alto the selection of Sir Charlm Dilke for a ministerial post outside the Cabinet. As Chief Secretary for Ireland the appeint- meat of Mr. Forster is favourably regarded by the Irish people, and the office he held in 1574, an Vice-President of the Council, in filled by Mr. Mundell, whose selection for ministerial distinction will he gratifying not only to his own constituents but to the Liberal party generally. Mr. J. G. Dodson eueeeeds to the office of Preaident of the Local Government Board. and Mr. Fawcett becomes the Post- master-General, while Mr. Bright, who takes office m Chancellor of the Duchy of lancaster, will lat a tower of strength in the newly-formed Cabinet.

The custom of delivering courses of sermons seems to be a somewhat popular one amongst the ministers in Runcorn district. One of the dangers to which preachers, who have a fondness for thin non of thing, are liable, in that they are very apt, unless they happen to be men of great range of mind, to keep reiterating ideas which they have brought before their congregation on previous Sabbaths, and to in. ilulge In a series of minute di ri r ions of their discourses such as are to be found in the tome, of old divinm, the only use of which, with rare exception', in to adorn the shelves of I some bibliopole or bibliomaniac. The apostle Paul looked upon the Church of Christ as a building to be put up and ! il umieinter is constantly engaged in putting up saffolding and never deals with such things as what I may denominate ! spiritual corner-stone or capital work, the structure with which he ha. to do is very likely to present a somewhat queer appearance. To any one who may ham such a mania.. I thought him entitled to. On the eve of a communion ! Sabbath, when assisting a brother clergyman in the same presbytery, one of the series wae delivered. •hich the minieter's ears had listened to oftener than Ile wished. - - THE "ETERNAL Rein" AOIIN.-At the meeting of the new Parliament on Thursday afternoon the two Hou.s of the I,egislature were the acetic of considerable animation, contrasting let marked degree with the languor and Indifference which had marked the opening of the final session favoured with the presenee of a Tory majority. Comparative calm continued, however, to prevail in the Peers' Chamber, to which, like a wandering Peri excluded unexpectedly from paradise, Mr. Raikes, once a high official of the State, anxiously sought admiseion at an early hour. Rumour had it that the ex-Chairman of Ways and Means was not disposed to he content with any less dignified position than a hinting on the steps of the throne itself, from which the coverings had been removed in preparation for the approaching ceresnenial, and that. on bein, told that he could not he allowed on this occasion to occupy the desired coign of vantage, the rejected of Chester informed the astounded official that he had become a "right honourable." l'he attendant, trembling hut faithful to duty, explained that as the Royal Commissioners were about to 'ensemble in front f the supposititious seat of authority the right honourable gentleman could not enter the enclosure usually reserved for Privy Councillors and Mr. Raikee, overruled on • point of o-der and privilege, sadly aotight a place in one 9I the side galle, les upstairs, whence ,he grimly surveyed the Howe below.—.Noncites fer Gvardran.

Peter Shaw, which took place on Saturday morning last. , Although his life was not marked by any particularly re-1 markable events, yet he was nine of those patient, consistent, I loom:. bard-working Christian men whom the world on ill afford to Irate. At the early age of 10 years, l'eter Shaw became dependent upon his men exertions for his daily bread. When SI years of age he entered the service of the London and North-Western Railway Company, and at the time of his death he had completed his :33r0 year in their employ. When about. 18 years of age he became • member of the timt Juvenile Temperance Society founded in Warring- ton, and from that time until his last Rine, laid him aside he was a most enthusiastic and hard-working advocate of total abstinence principles. In all movements which hail for their object the social, political, or religious elevation of his fellows he for many years took • most active par Land the coosiatent character of his private life added consider- , ably to the influence which he ntherwiee exercised. During his illness, which was at times most painful, he evinced the I most cheerful patience and Christian fortitude; end while we mourn for our loss, we cannot but rejoice in knowing Ile in now with those of whom it is void, "These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their rol.en End made them white in the blood of the Lamb.' Ten PUNE or BUCCINTON'S PRIER CATTLE DISQUALI FIND. • —At the aoimal open show, held at Ayr, on Wednesday, • under the auspices of the Ayrshire Agricultural Association, quite sensation W.I. created by the judges disqualifying three animalr belonging to the Duke of Buccleuch on the ground of having been doctored. The clam for which the animals were entered was the principal one of the show. It has bren alleged for some years that exhibitor, have been tempering with the Mats of the cows shown, the object being to prevent the outflow of milk. To pot down this practice measures were recently taken by the management, but no case for some years has been detected by the inspec. tors until Wednesday, when three of his Grace's finest cows were found to have been tightly hound with tape round the teate. The Duke's representative protested, but the com- mittee remained firm, and the animals were ordered out of the judging ring. Smith, jun., read an interesting paper on "The discoveries made by M. M. Frederic Moreau in the ancient cemetery of Caranda, in the department of the Aisne, France."—A vete of thanks was accorded to Mr. Smith for his paper,and the meeting terminated.

Nemo writes front Lymm Sc follows :—Now that the geneml election is over, ! I think the Liberals of Lvmm should look a little moreafter : extending their principles, and adopt the bent means of doing the same. The litat thing it to obtain the names of those who are qualified to vote but at present are not on the register. Induce such persons to attend at the revision court 10 substantiate their clahns to be put on the register. I understand there has been much diffidence on the part of voters attending the revision court consequent upon the authority which Tory officials have arrogated to themselves when in attendance at the court. Such arrogance deserves severe reprobation, I would certainly advise those who have not s vote, but who are qualitied,—and especially I ,oking at the result of the ant Mid-Cheshire election—that they would best serve their own enls and the country In,eeing , to the register at the proper time.—The second Matter to I which I would call attention is the went of a Lite at Cluh, I where young men could meet and express their opinions on the great and momentous questions of the day which are continu illy cropping up, and where Liberal literature could be disseminated at • slight end trifling cost. Recently you recorded the opening of A Conservative Club St Sale; why should we be thus behind in Lymm in starting a club? Surely the Liberal gentlemen in this district would not be behind in siding such an object, which would ha,-e the ad• vantage of .removing the ignorance and politiml blindness at present exlsting in the minds of many of the voters of the I,y,mrn polling district.—Nano... ss.

A petition, bearing seveml thousand signatures, has reached Constantinople. It is in- tended to be presented to the Sultan. The signatories are all Albanians. div.p: ST. HELENS PAIILIAMENTARy DEBATING SOCIETY.

The Inaugural meeting of a society bearing the adore title in connection with the St. Helens Liberal Association, xan held on Thursday evening in the Cominittee.rsom of the Liberal Club. Ildr society, which owes its inception to , the efforts of the junior members principally of the club, is composed purely of members connected with the associetiou, and is intended to cultivate not only the art of oratory, but to develop an iatimate know helge with the political history of the timer. Although composed of men of Liberal views. the interests of the Opposition will not be neglecied. as several will champion the cause of Conservatism, and thus elicit debateable matter. It is natural, however, that, seeing its intimate connection with one section of politicans. thai the members composing the seciely and 11110 are to brest. lances on the Conservative side, will not enter into it with the saute :est as would he the case with • real Simon pure." The meeting the other evening not only met, however, to frame rules and elect °nicer,, but to hear an exeellent paper which was tend by the Rev. It. J. Weallierhead. of St. Helens The chair was occupied hy Mr. W. J. Marrow, and there were also present—The Rev. H. J. I.Veatherhead, Menu!, T. Rabin, lironigoole, Stephenson, J. Lockland,R.Belsher, Jon J. Barb IWI ton, AMulet. Booth, J. T. Elmwood, Crompton. W. Boyle, R. Clarke, E. Igningoole, F. Dromgoole, Cotton, R. G. Brook, Dewar, T. Monet ieff, C. Tinker (bon. Beastlier I. and J. B. Mean. (bon. secretary). The subject of the paper was 0 The new Parliament, and its probable work." Mr. Weatherbead, in his opening remarks, very cleverly disposed of the objection raised that ministers of religion should net interfere with politien, aud then proceeded to speak of the recently elected Parliament. lie congratulated the Lit oral party on their accession to power, and haring placed at their head one of the abled financiers and the cleverest statesman the world ever produced. (Cheers.) He enumerated the different bills wiEch would prolgtily , occupy the attention of the new Government. Having now got rid of Imperialism, the day star of their hope was then again, and shined resplendent in the clear sky, a system , which coclaimed itself a Government of Ignorant statesmen , had beet cut short, and the °overturn nt of the people, by the people and from the people, had become more firmly established than before when Gladstone, Bright, Harlington. Granville, and other good men and true in the Cabinet. and with such A phalanx of earneet and true Liberals in the ; House of Commons they would see revived In English life the best traditions of their paet history, and 1. England would once inore stand forth maintaining a policy which ahould rest an the unchanging foundation of Christian morality, and should be again • - - -
•. The far. eof the happy ; an,l of the free; Flower of the oevan gem of the sea."

On one occasion a little boy, 10 years of age, actually en.. Allowed to take oaths upon his lips. He stopped the piece and turned the word off as hest he could. He thought that more care ought to be exercised in the selection of re- citations and dialogues, and that they ought to be passed by some responsible person. Mr. flokus of klanchester, agreed with what had been said, but at the same time amusement should he provided for the children in order to make them merry. Laughter was. very good thing,and if lie could buy a bushel he would do so. Amusement, of course, could be provided without anything of d demoralising tendency Accompanying it, and he fully appreciated the necessity of something being done in this respect. _ . .

PUBLIC MEETING.

In the evening a public meeting was he'd in the Town Hall, presided over by Mr. E. Shorroclus Eccles, of Huvton, and among there present were Captain Balantine, the itevs. T. I'. Lambert (Liverpool), H. J. Weatherhead, T. Wit- shaw, W. C. Taller, and T. I'. Spencer ) Messrs. Jneob Earnehaw (Manchester), and J. B. Leach (preeident of the St. Helens Band of Hope Union). ••

The ettetuvme, who mid he wee • total ahetainer, though he had not always been one, spoke of the evils arieing from intemperance in every community and in every grade of society. Referring to a letter in the nompapers from Mr. Hoyle, of Bury, he was glad to rind that the drink Bill of 1879 had decreased 14,000,001 below that of the pre- ceding year. The consumption of [es had gone up, there- fore the drinking of the people had only Wen transferred from one article to another. 'The recent elections bad been I instrumental M turning several brewers out of the House of Commons. lie hoped that the brewing interest would decrease year by year, and that the temperance party would have more and more power. Many men deeply interested in the temperance cause had been returned to Parliament and that spoke a great deal. Ile thought they aught also take heart from the way in which the cocoa rooms were progressing. (Hear, hear.) He went on to say that they wanted children to have good reasons for being total abstainers, and those who were taking interest in that movement niust try to give good remone to the children tor what they were teaching them. He was very glad that no runny hooka were being irmed in regas3 to alcohol. tin. HiChArilPoi. had done very great work. (Hear, hear.) The simplest child could understand he books, and he hoped the tittin would come when tomb booke were put into their echools, mad made port of the curriculum. The Rev. T. T. LAUBER; in the course of an excellent addrem, mid that Lancashire was celebrated for four thing. —Sunday schools, tea meetings, cotton, and clogs. (Hear, hear.) He should also like to add Bands of Hope. He held that every chapel Fan incomplete without aSunday school, and every Sundry oohed was incomplete without a Band of 110.—(beer, hear); for one taught the grand principles of religion, and the other shielded or should shield them prin- ciples. There were some people who raid they must do their part towards mining the revenue, and that the Queen umst be supporter. He held, however, that their first duty was to Le loyal to their own queen at home. (Cheers.) 'There were scores of homes or St. Helene that night through whose windows sunlight had never glinted for months on • happiness and comfort, but only on wretchednem. equator, and want. Nothing made men look like demons more than among drink. Drink cost them 140,090,000 a year, and robbed 300.000 Englieh homer of their happinesa, and 10.000,001) British girls of their virtue. "I drink to make me work," mid a ',rung roan. "Ave,'' remarked an old man, ['her drink and tha' will have to work. !once drank make myself work. lam mventy years of age. I might have been independent, but now, mark you, lam obliged to work for my living. Drink lads and it will iflake network, and take you to the workhouse alter that." (Applaum.) He concluded a very interesting address by alluding to the new Parliament, composed as it was by a good many favourable , to the temperance movement, and he said that he did not think it would be long before they hod a Local Option Bill. On the Swift, , who appeared to proeecute, mid that up to the time of his apprehension the prisoner was deputy underlooker over one of the pits ; and it was part of his duty, when pay day came round, to give an account of the time made by the men who had been working under him. 'Their great work watt to reclaion the fallen, and to cove °them from falling victims to intemperance and they were pre- pared that night to enlist 'won@ into the ever- increasing army of teetotallers.
